package.name: Crypto
package.description: Cryptographic hashes, message authentication codes and key derivation

modules.name: Blake3
modules.header:
BLAKE3: the compression function, the chunk state, and the tree that joins chunks together.
BLAKE3 is a tree hash, and that is the whole of what makes it different. A message is cut into chunks of a
kibibyte; each chunk is compressed to a chaining value independently, and the chaining values are joined
pairwise up a binary tree until one remains. Nothing in that depends on the order the chunks are processed,
which is why the algorithm parallelizes — and it is also why the implementation is more intricate than a
sequential hash, since the tree has to be maintained rather than just a running state.
The tree is kept as a stack of subtree chaining values, and the trick that keeps it small is arithmetic: after
finishing the chunk at index n, the number of subtrees to merge is the number of trailing one bits in n. That
single fact replaces any bookkeeping about which subtrees are complete.
The flags carry the position information a tree hash needs and a sequential one does not. A chaining value
means nothing without knowing whether it came from the start of a chunk, the end of one, a parent node, or the
root — and mixing that into the compression is what stops one part of the tree being substituted for another.

modules.name: Blake3Modes
modules.header:
BLAKE3's other two modes, which are the same tree with a different starting key and a different flag.
The point of having modes at all is domain separation. The same bytes hashed unkeyed, hashed with a key, and
used as key material produce three unrelated outputs, and no amount of work with one mode says anything about
another. That is what lets one algorithm serve as a hash, as a message authentication code, and as a key
derivation function without the three interfering — which is otherwise the sort of thing that turns a
perfectly good hash into a vulnerability when someone uses it for two purposes at once.
Keyed hashing is a MAC, and a proper one: BLAKE3 is not vulnerable to length extension, so unlike SHA-2 it can
be keyed by simply starting from the key rather than needing HMAC's nested construction.

modules.name: Digest
modules.header:
What a digest is, and the two operations every user of one gets wrong.
**This package has not been independently reviewed.** Every algorithm matches its published vectors, and that
is a weaker statement than it sounds: the failures that matter in cryptographic code — a comparison that
leaks timing, a secret that outlives its use, a construction applied outside the assumptions it was proved
under — all pass vectors without complaint. Until a review by someone who did not write this is recorded,
nothing here should be relied on where an adversary is in the picture.
A digest is used incrementally far more often than in one call — a file is hashed as it is read, a message as
it is assembled — so the incremental form is the contract and the one-shot form is written on top of it,
rather than the other way round. `Update` may be called any number of times with any split of the same bytes
and must produce the same digest, which is a stronger promise than it looks: it is what lets a caller change
its buffer size without changing its output.
The other two operations are here because they are the ones callers reach for from the standard library and
find something subtly unsuitable. Comparing two digests with an ordinary loop returns as soon as it finds a
difference, so how long it takes reveals where the difference is — and an attacker who can time a tag check
can find the right tag one byte at a time, which is thousands of guesses instead of astronomically many.
Clearing a secret with an ordinary loop is dead code to a compiler, since nothing reads the buffer afterwards,
and it is entitled to remove it.

modules.name: Hkdf
modules.header:
HKDF: turning a shared secret into as many keys as a protocol needs.
The two steps do different jobs and it matters which is which. Extract takes input keying material that may be
biased — a Diffie-Hellman shared secret is a group element, not a uniform string — and concentrates whatever
entropy it has into one fixed-length pseudorandom key. Expand takes that key and stretches it to any length,
separated by an info string so that keys for different purposes are unrelated. Skipping extract because the
input "looks random enough" is the common mistake, and it is the step that makes the rest sound.
The salt is not a secret and does not need to be unpredictable — a protocol identifier or a session
transcript is ideal. It is what stops two protocols deriving the same keys from the same secret. The info
string does the same job one level down, between purposes within one protocol.
The length limit is real and not a formality: expand produces at most 255 blocks, because the counter it feeds
into each round is a single byte. Asking for more has no answer, so this refuses rather than repeating.

modules.name: Hmac
modules.header:
HMAC: a message authentication code built from any digest that has a block size.
The construction exists because the obvious thing does not work. Hashing a key followed by a message is not a
MAC for any Merkle-Damgard hash — SHA-1, SHA-2, MD5 — because such a hash's output *is* its internal state,
so anyone holding a tag can continue hashing from it and produce a valid tag for a longer message without ever
learning the key. HMAC's nesting is what closes that: the outer hash sees only a fixed-length input, so its
state is never exposed in a form that can be extended.
The two pads are what make the inner and outer hashes use different keys, and they are different in every bit
pair, which is what keeps the two derived keys from being related in a way that helps an attacker.
Not needed for BLAKE3 or SHA-3, which resist length extension and can be keyed directly — but supported for
them anyway, since a protocol that specifies HMAC specifies HMAC.

modules.name: Keccak
modules.header:
Keccak-f[1600] and the four SHA-3 hashes built on it.
SHA-3 is not a Merkle-Damgard hash like SHA-2. There is no compression function taking a chaining value and a
block: there is a permutation over a fixed 1600-bit state, and a message is absorbed into part of that state a
rate at a time and then squeezed back out. The part that is never touched directly by the message is the
capacity, and it is what the security level is set by — which is why the four hashes differ only in how much
of the state they expose, not in their permutation.
That structure makes SHA-3 immune to the length-extension attack SHA-2 permits, because the output squeezed
out is a window onto a state the attacker cannot complete. It is the reason to reach for SHA-3 over SHA-2 when
a raw hash is used where a MAC belongs.

modules.name: Legacy
modules.header:
MD5 and SHA-1, kept only for the formats and protocols that will not change.
**Both are broken and neither should be chosen for anything new.** MD5 collisions can be produced in seconds
on a laptop, and have been used to forge certificates; SHA-1 collisions were demonstrated in 2017 and cost far
less now. Neither offers collision resistance, so neither can be used for a signature, a content address, a
deduplication key, or anything else where two different inputs producing one output is a problem.
What they remain usable for is reading what already exists: a legacy file format, a protocol handshake that
cannot be renegotiated, a checksum in a system nobody will update. The names carry `Legacy` so that reaching
for one is a decision a reader can see, and so that a search for "Sha1" in a codebase finds every place the
decision was made.
Neither is a `Digest` implementation, deliberately. A generic function taking any digest should not silently
accept these, and code that wants one must name it.

modules.name: Sha256
modules.header:
SHA-256 and SHA-224, from FIPS 180-4.
One compression function serves both: they differ only in the initial state and in how much of the final
state is kept. That is worth saying plainly, because it is also why SHA-224 is not simply "SHA-256 truncated"
— a different initial state means the two produce unrelated values, so neither can be derived from the other
after the fact.
The padding is where implementations go wrong, and it is the same shape in every member of the family: a one
bit, then zeros, then the message length in bits as a big-endian 64-bit count. The awkward case is a message
whose final block leaves fewer than nine bytes free, which needs a whole extra block; the test covers exactly
those lengths.

modules.name: Sha512
modules.header:
SHA-512 and its three truncations, from FIPS 180-4.
The same shape as SHA-256 one size up: sixty-four bit words, eighty rounds, blocks of a hundred and twenty
eight bytes, and a length count of a hundred and twenty eight bits. The rotation amounts and shift distances
differ, and so does everything derived from them; nothing here is SHA-256 with a wider type.
Four functions share the compression: SHA-512 keeps all eight words, SHA-384 keeps six, and SHA-512/224 and
SHA-512/256 keep the first twenty-eight and thirty-two bytes. Each starts from a different initial state --
the truncations' states are themselves derived by hashing their own names, which is what stops any of them
from being a prefix of another. A caller who wants a short digest from a long one must use these rather than
cutting SHA-512 down, since cutting it down gives a value with a known relationship to the full digest.

modules.name: Shake
modules.header:
SHAKE128 and SHAKE256: the same sponge, squeezed for as long as the caller wants.
A hash gives a fixed number of bytes because that is what a hash is for. An extendable-output function gives
as many as asked, from the same absorbed state, as one continuous stream — so `Read` twice for sixteen bytes
gives exactly what `Read` once for thirty-two gives. That property is the whole contract, and it is what makes
these usable as key-stream generators and as the expansion step of a key derivation.
The number in the name is the security level, not the output length: SHAKE128 offers 128 bits of security
however many bytes are taken from it, and taking more does not add any. Nothing enforces that, because there
is no length at which it becomes wrong — only a length past which it stops helping.
The domain byte is what separates these from SHA-3. The same state absorbing the same message produces a
different stream depending on that one byte, which is what stops a SHAKE output from ever colliding with a
SHA-3 digest by construction.

doc.summary: A keyed BLAKE3 hash: a message authentication code.
doc.markdown:
A keyed BLAKE3 hash: a message authentication code.
`key` must be exactly thirty-two bytes; a shorter one is padded with zeros, which is a caller error
rather than a supported shortening — a key with less entropy than the algorithm expects is weaker than
it looks, and padding it hides that rather than fixing it.
Unlike SHA-2, this needs no nested construction: BLAKE3 resists length extension, so starting the tree
from the key is a sound MAC on its own.
doc.returns: a hasher keyed with those thirty-two bytes

doc.summary: A BLAKE3 state deriving output under `context`.
doc.markdown:
A BLAKE3 state deriving output under `context`.
The context string names what the derived key is *for*, and it is hashed separately from the key
material so that two derivations from the same material under different contexts are unrelated. It
should be a hard-coded, globally unique string — an application name, a purpose, and a date — and it
must not be a variable, since two callers who accidentally share one lose the separation entirely.

params.name: context
params.markdown: the application-specific context string, which must be a constant

doc.returns: a hasher in key-derivation mode for that context

items.name: Equal
items.signature: pub func Equal(left: char8[..], right: char8[..]) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether two byte sequences are equal, in time that does not depend on where they differ.
doc.markdown:
Whether two byte sequences are equal, in time that does not depend on where they differ.
The ordinary comparison returns at the first difference, so its duration reveals the length of the matching
prefix. Against a message authentication tag that is enough to find the correct tag one byte at a time --
a few thousand attempts rather than the number the tag's length suggests. This reads every byte of both
sequences whatever it finds, accumulating differences rather than branching on them.
Sequences of different lengths are unequal, and that answer is immediate: a length is not a secret, and
pretending otherwise would mean reading past one of them.

params.name: left
params.markdown: one of the two byte runs

doc.returns: whether the two runs match, compared in time that does not depend on where they differ

items.name: Wipe
items.signature: pub func Wipe(bytes: var char8[..])

doc.summary: Overwrites `bytes` with zeros in a way the compiler may not remove.
doc.markdown:
Overwrites `bytes` with zeros in a way the compiler may not remove.
A plain loop clearing a buffer nothing reads afterwards is dead code, and an optimizer is entitled to delete
it — which is how a key a program believed it had erased stays in memory, in a core dump, or in a page
written to swap. The barrier below is handed the buffer's address and its body is opaque, so the writes must
have happened before it runs and the call cannot be dropped.

doc.summary: Writes the digest into `into`.

Writes the digest into `into`.

count. When fewer than nine bytes remain in the final block there is no room for that count, so the
block is finished with zeros and a whole further block carries it — the case that separates a correct
implementation from one that passes the short vectors.

doc.summary: Absorbs `bytes` into the state.
doc.markdown:
Absorbs `bytes` into the state.
Absorbing after reading has begun is a caller error: the stream is a function of everything absorbed
before the first read, and adding to it afterwards would silently change what a caller already has. This
ignores such a call rather than corrupting the stream.
